We're happy to announce that ThyVoice, our state-of-the-art approach to solving "who said what" across conversations at 10x lower cost, has been accepted at IEEE SLT 2026.

ThyVoice outperforms the top 8 speech systems, including those built with OpenAI, ElevenLabs, Deepgram, AssemblyAI, and pyannoteAI, as well as academic baselines.

"Who said what" sounds simple, but it's actually two hard problems stacked together:

- Diarization: splitting a recording by speaker - Speaker ID: recognizing the same person across conversations

If either one fails, the result is incorrect attribution and polluted data.

Our contribution is twofold. First, we introduce a new metric, Speaker-Identified cpWER (SI-cpWER). Second, we present ThyVoice, which achieves the best SI-cpWER on CHiME-8 NOTSOFAR and CHiME-6, benchmarks that simulate real-world meetings and noisy environments.

The key insight of our work is that pooling all samples of the same speaker across a recording performs better than using embeddings from the largest single sub-sample. We also present a larger system that orchestrates this as a multi-step process: removing overlapping speech, stitching together each speaker's audio, and matching it against a speaker bank.

More details are in the linked arxiv pre-print.

> Her argument claimed that while we perceived legible text coming from ChatGPT, we were actually being fooled by our innate pattern-matching instincts

This is an accurate summary, I think, and the point the authors are making sits somewhere in the coordinate space of a simplified reframing of the Chinese Room, Grice's account of intention in meaning, Wittgenstein's "Say 'It's cold here' and mean 'It's warm here'" challenge, and a whole bunch of the hermeneutic tradition.

Very roughly, you might say that an LLM doesn't mean anything when it emits text, but that the text still has meaning (which I think is all tptacek wants from "meaningful outputs", but you could take that further as culturally or scientifically 'meaningful', i.e. 'significant').

Philosophically, there are people who hold the position that something has to have been meant to have meaning, or that something has to have meaning in the first place to be meant, and so on. There were always interesting edge cases to these accounts (actors delivering lines, or the Dada/Burroughs cut-up technique), but LLMs are challenging in a way that e.g. Racter wasn't.

"Stochastic parrot" is a fitting term for this because the parrot's words have meaning, but the parrot itself doesn't mean anything by them. Not literally, anyway. And that's it. That's the whole analogy.

Most website implementations that support passkeys have to support multiple key enrollment. It's the only long-term reliable way for the many, many users that are cross-ecosystem, which especially means Windows users in the age of no Windows Phone. Every Windows user has either an Android or iPhone. You can bootstrap with Bluetooth LTE access to your phone for a Passkey, but it's a rough web experience if the user needs to do that every time they access a page, so most good flows ask the user the enroll a Windows PC passkey in addition to their phone's passkey and really good ones make use of a passkey auto-enrollment option designed for this scenario (Bluetooth passkey to "local" passkey auto-enrollment).

Perhaps surprisingly, Windows has helped keep Passkeys from being "proprietary" lock-in because Microsoft no longer has users in a single ecosystem.

There is no dedicated auto-enrollment for "backup" keys, but most consumer sites make it very easy to enroll "backup" keys yourself.

Also, Passkeys don't have to be "online" to enroll additional keys. Each key is independent, enrolling is just generating new keys. The trouble is that web browsers generate lots of Passkeys (at least one per domain, at the very least) so if you in theory want to print them all and store them in a physical vault it might be a hefty book you are printing.

Cloud sync isn't required. Most users want it so that they don't have a single-point-of-failure.

As an implementation detail some Passkeys have a master key that is then used in some key derivation function (KDF) to generate the hundreds or thousands of individual passkeys (at least one per domain), and that's what most Yubikey passkey implementations need to do because Yubikeys weren't designed to store lots of keys, so it is devices like Yubikey that makes it seem like Passkeys are less independent than they really are.
